title: When the Teacher Peeks: Answer-Conditioned Chains Degrade Reasoning Distillation

body:
The usual recipe for making a smaller model think like a larger one has three steps. Sample reasoning traces from a strong teacher. Keep the ones whose final answer is correct. Fine-tune the student on what you kept. The filter is the quality guarantee: if the answer is right, the chain that produced it is safe to copy. That premise has been load-bearing for every recent "R1-distilled Qwen", every "s1K-tuned 32B", every open-weights reasoning release of the last year. A new preprint argues the premise is wrong in a specific, measurable, and recoverable way (Lee et al., 2026). The chains are not safe just because the answers are.

The attack surface it names is answer conditioning. When the teacher fails to produce a correct chain for a hard problem, a common workaround — folded, often silently, into dataset pipelines — is to show the teacher the gold answer and ask for a chain that reaches it. The chains survive the correctness filter by construction. They also, the paper shows, encode a reasoning strategy that works backward from a known target. A student fine-tuned on them does worse on verifiable reasoning, worse the harder the problem, and worse in a way the filter cannot detect.

## Why this matters now

The current frontier of open reasoning models leans heavily on supervised fine-tuning on long chains sampled from a stronger model. DeepSeek-R1 distilled six dense student models by SFT alone on hundreds of thousands of curated traces (DeepSeek-AI, 2025). s1 reached a budget-forcing-controlled version of o1-preview-level MATH and AIME24 performance with 1,000 traces, under $50 of compute, and no RL (Muennighoff et al., 2025). Both pipelines treat a trace as a unit — if the answer verifies, the trace enters the training set. Both are explicit that teacher samples are regenerated when they fail. The regeneration step is where answer conditioning quietly enters. If you re-prompt the teacher with the correct answer in context, you convert an answer-blind sample from $P(y_{1:T} \mid x)$ into an answer-conditioned sample from $P(y_{1:T} \mid x, a^\*)$. Both yield traces ending in $a^\*$, so both clear the filter. They are not the same distribution over chains.

## Two conditionals that collide at the final token

Fix a problem $x$ with gold answer $a^\*$. Let $y_{1:T}$ be a candidate chain whose last token encodes an answer $a(y)$. The honest distribution the student would like to learn is the posterior under correct termination,

$$P_B(y_{1:T} \mid x, a(y) = a^\*) \;\propto\; P(y_{1:T} \mid x) \,\mathbb{1}[a(y)=a^\*],$$

which is just Bayes' rule applied to the teacher's unconditional policy. This is the distribution you actually get when you sample without the answer and reject failures. Call it answer-blind.

The other distribution — the one you get by injecting $a^\*$ into the prompt — is

$$P_A(y_{1:T} \mid x, a^\*) \;=\; \prod_t P_\theta(y_t \mid y_{<t}, x, a^\*).$$

Here the teacher attends to $a^\*$ at every step. The autoregressive factorization means every intermediate token can be chosen to be *compatible with* $a^\*$, not merely to be a step on the way to it. The two conditionals coincide only in a degenerate case: when $P(y_{1:T} \mid x)$ already assigns almost all its mass to chains that reach $a^\*$. On easy problems that happens routinely. On the problems where answer conditioning gets used — the ones where the teacher fails without a hint — it does not.

The structural tell is temporal: under $P_B$ the model does not know $a^\*$ at step $t$, so it cannot encode it in $y_t$ for $t \ll T$. Under $P_A$ it does, and often does. The paper measures this with a simple diagnostic, the fraction of traces whose first stated final answer appears far before the end. Under answer conditioning that fraction climbs sharply. Under answer-blind sampling it stays flat.

## The empirical result

Lee et al. (2026) hold the generator, the problem set, and the correctness filter fixed, and vary only whether the teacher sees $a^\*$. Every trace in both arms clears the same answer check. They then fine-tune eight thinking models drawn from four families on each arm separately and evaluate on verifiable-reasoning benchmarks.

Training on answer-conditioned chains lowers MATH-500 accuracy by about 16 points relative to training on the same number of answer-blind chains. On the hardest competition problems — AIME-level — the gap reaches about 27 points. The effect is monotone in difficulty: the easier the problem the smaller the gap, which is consistent with the mechanism above (on easy problems the two conditionals are closer). The eight models span base scales and families, which rules out a single-architecture artifact.

A parallel finding appears in medicine. Jiang et al. (2026) distilled a Qwen3-8B student from a DeepSeek-V3-family teacher on MedQA-USMLE and reported self-consistency@64 rising from 74.7% to 84.4%. The step-level audit went the other way: the error rate on non-abstained reasoning steps rose from 30.6% to 50.3%, and a blind clinician audit of 150 steps reproduced the ordering. The teacher had been passed the answer during generation.

## A concrete anchor

Consider a two-step arithmetic problem: $x =$ "$17 \times 13 + 5 = ?$", $a^\* = 226$. Answer-blind sampling produces chains that compute $17 \times 13 = 221$, then $221 + 5 = 226$, then emit $226$. Answer conditioning allows chains that notice $226 - 5 = 221$ and $221 = 17 \times 13$ and write the derivation in forward order anyway, having worked back. On this problem the difference is invisible: both end at 226 and both look like valid arithmetic. The problem is that the second kind of chain teaches the student a policy whose first move is to produce an answer and justify it, rather than to derive one. On a problem the student cannot work backward from — a competition problem where the search space is not invertible — that policy produces an early plausible answer followed by rationalization, which the correctness filter at inference time catches as wrong.

The following sketch is enough to run the audit locally on any trace dump:

```python
import re

ANS = re.compile(r"\\boxed\{([^}]*)\}|the answer is ([^.\n]+)", re.I)

def first_answer_position(trace: str) -> float | None:
    """Return the fractional position (0..1) of the first final-answer statement.
    None if the trace never commits to an answer in a boxed/explicit form."""
    hits = [(m.start(), m.group(1) or m.group(2)) for m in ANS.finditer(trace)]
    if not hits:
        return None
    return hits[0][0] / max(len(trace), 1)

def early_answer_rate(traces, threshold=0.5):
    positions = [first_answer_position(t) for t in traces]
    positions = [p for p in positions if p is not None]
    return sum(p < threshold for p in positions) / len(positions)
```

Run this on an answer-blind dump and an answer-conditioned dump. The ratio of the two early-answer rates is the data-level fingerprint. The paper's point is that this ratio is visible *before* fine-tuning, so a dataset can be audited for the harm it will cause.

## What it implies in practice

Three things. First, treat the trace, not just the answer, as the unit of correctness. A trace is a sample from one of two different conditionals, and the correctness filter cannot tell them apart. Second, log the generation condition. Any trace in a reasoning SFT corpus should carry a provenance flag: was the teacher shown the answer. If the flag is missing, assume the worst. Third, prefer answer-blind pipelines even at the cost of fewer traces. The AIME-27-point gap is large enough that one answer-blind trace is worth more than several answer-conditioned ones. A derivative of this is to use the early-answer-position statistic as a filter: traces whose first final-answer statement lands in the first half of the chain are suspect regardless of how they were produced.

The deeper lesson is about where shortcuts enter the pipeline. Turpin et al. (2023) and Lanham et al. (2023) established that chain-of-thought explanations can be unfaithful to the computation that produced the answer — the chain is a post-hoc rationalization even when the model generates it unprompted. Arcuschin et al. (2025) extend this to frontier models in the wild. Answer conditioning is the industrial version of the same bug: unfaithfulness manufactured deliberately, by prompt design, and then packaged as training data.

## Limits and open questions

Several. The result is correlational on the step level — the audit measures where the final answer first appears, which is a proxy for working-backward reasoning, not a direct observation of it. Faithfulness metrics are themselves contested; Bentham et al. (2024) show that at least one popular family of faithfulness scores confounds unfaithfulness with answer-choice bias. We do not know whether answer conditioning is the only reasoning-data pathology or whether any shortcut-rich distribution (e.g., process-reward-model-filtered chains that select for brevity) produces similar effects. The eight-model, four-family evidence is broad on scales but shallow on tasks: the audit should be redone on code and on scientific-reasoning benchmarks where "verifiable" means something subtler than a numeric answer match. And the audit is defensive — it tells you a dataset is compromised. The constructive question, which the paper does not fully answer, is how to recover chains for problems the teacher cannot solve blind without reintroducing the shortcut. Possibilities include majority-voting over many answer-blind samples, process-level reward models trained to reward derivation rather than termination, and RL with verifiable rewards (as in R1-Zero) that bypasses the SFT distillation step entirely but costs orders of magnitude more compute.

Verifiable rewards do not make the problem go away either; they relocate it. A verifier that checks only the final answer leaves the chain unconstrained, so a long-horizon RL run can discover its own answer-conditioned shortcuts without a teacher's help. The question of what, exactly, a chain is for — and what a dataset of chains should preserve — is still open.

## Further reading

- Lee, J. et al. (2026). *Answer-Conditioned Chains of Thought Degrade Verifiable-Reasoning Distillation in Large Language Models.* arXiv:2607.14552. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14552>. The paper this post is built on; the one-bit experiment and the 16/27-point gaps are from it.
- Jiang, Z., Peng, X., Teng, F., Fu, Z., Kim, Y., Mi, J., Li, Z., Wu, H. (2026). *Better Accuracies, Worse Reasoning: A Step-Level Audit of Medical Chain-of-Thought Distillation.* arXiv:2605.28301. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28301>. The medical parallel: SC@64 up, step-level error up, in the same distillation.
- DeepSeek-AI (2025). *DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning.* arXiv:2501.12948. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948>. The reference distillation pipeline the attack surface in this post applies to.
- Muennighoff, N. et al. (2025). *s1: Simple Test-Time Scaling.* arXiv:2501.19393. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393>. The 1,000-trace, under-$50 distillation recipe; a near-worst case for a hidden-shortcut dataset given its small size.
- Turpin, M., Michael, J., Perez, E., Bowman, S.R. (2023). *Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting.* arXiv:2305.04388. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04388>. The canonical demonstration that CoT text can be a post-hoc rationalization rather than a derivation.
- Lanham, T. et al. (2023). *Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning.* arXiv:2307.13702. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.13702>. Interventional faithfulness tests; the non-monotonic scaling of faithfulness.
- Arcuschin, I. et al. (2025). *Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in the Wild Is Not Always Faithful.* arXiv:2503.08679. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.08679>. "Unfaithful Illogical Shortcuts" in frontier reasoning models; the field evidence that supports the backward-chain mechanism.
- Hinton, G., Vinyals, O., Dean, J. (2015). *Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network.* arXiv:1503.02531. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531>. The original formulation of distillation; useful to re-read because the modern reasoning version replaces soft targets with hard-answer-filtered sampled traces, which is where the data-vs-model confusion starts.
